prayer.text: First Roman Martyrs, pray for us.

cues.text: Rome in Flames
In July of AD 64, a catastrophic fire tore through Rome , destroying much of the city over the course of six days.
Rumor quickly spread that Emperor Nero himself had ordered the blaze, whether to clear space for his own architectural ambitions or from simple indifference to the suffering it caused.
The enduring image of Nero 'fiddling while Rome burned,' though likely more legend than fact, reflects the depth of public suspicion that fell on him.
Blame Shifted to the Christians
Alarmed by the growing popular anger directed at him, Nero moved to deflect blame onto the small, poorly understood Christian community already present in the city.
The Roman historian Tacitus , no friend to Christianity himself, records Nero’s persecution of Christians as a class hated for their abominations.
His account provides direct outside confirmation, from a hostile pagan source, of the persecution’s basic facts.
Torments Recorded by Tacitus
According to Tacitus's account, the condemned Christians were killed in deliberately theatrical and horrifying ways.
Some were sewn into wild-animal skins and torn apart by dogs in the public arena, while others were crucified.
Still others were coated in pitch and set alight as living torches, illuminating Nero's own gardens after dark and providing grim entertainment for an evening spectacle.
Peter, Paul, and a Multitude
Tradition holds that Saints Peter and Paul also died under Nero.
Their feast on June 29 comes immediately before the memorial of these first martyrs in the Church's calendar.
The Roman Martyrology calls the unnamed victims 'the first fruits of the martyrs' that the Roman Church 'offered to God before the death of the Apostles'.
In other words, this multitude was martyred first, and the Apostles followed them.
A Multitude Without Names
Unlike many early martyrs whose individual names and stories the Church has preserved, ordinary Christians killed in Nero's persecution of 64 are remembered collectively.
Their identities were lost to history, even as the later Roman historian Tacitus described the fact and manner of their deaths.
Tacitus, a pagan writer, included details of the punishment inflicted on Christians.
Legacy
This feast was added to the General Roman Calendar only in the 1969 reform.
It gives liturgical recognition to this vast, unnamed company of early Roman believers.
Placed immediately after the solemnity of Peter and Paul, this deliberate reminder affirms the early Roman Church's foundation in blood.
It was not the work of its most famous martyrs alone, but of countless ordinary Christians whose names are known only to God.
